questions.passage: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction inside their abdomens. An enzyme called luciferase helps a compound called luciferin combine with oxygen, releasing energy as light with almost no heat. Each species flashes in its own pattern, and these patterns help males and females of the same species find one another in the dark. Some predatory fireflies copy the flash of another species to lure males close, and then eat them. Scientists are studying the reaction because such efficient light could inspire better lamps and medical tests.

options: Why Lamps Waste So Much Heat
Fireflies Found Only in Dark Places

questions.explanation: The passage explains how the light is produced, how flashes serve mating, and why it interests scientists.

questions.passage: Antibiotics treat infections caused by bacteria, not by viruses. Colds and influenza are viral, so taking antibiotics for them offers no benefit. Worse, each unnecessary dose gives surviving bacteria a chance to adapt, producing strains that no longer respond to the drug. Health workers call this antimicrobial resistance, and it is now regarded as one of the greatest threats to modern medicine, since routine surgery and cancer treatment both depend on antibiotics to prevent infection. Patients should therefore take antibiotics only when prescribed and should finish the full course.

options: Viruses are more dangerous than bacteria.
Doctors should avoid prescribing any medicine.
Colds can be cured by antibiotics.
Surgery is no longer safe for anyone.
Antibiotics should be used only when needed because misuse leads to resistant bacteria.
questions.explanation: The passage warns against unnecessary use and explains resistance.

questions.passage: Between 1946 and 1948, the young Philippine Republic faced a heavy task of rebuilding. Manila had been among the most devastated cities of the Second World War, and farms, roads, and schools across the islands lay in ruins. The government depended on foreign aid and war-damage payments, but these funds arrived slowly and often did not match the scale of the destruction. Some historians argue that the delay allowed corruption and unrest to take root, while others stress that the new nation simply lacked experienced institutions. Both views agree on one point: recovery was far harder than the leaders of independence had expected.
questions.question: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The causes of the Second World War
The difficulties of rebuilding the Philippines after the war
The success of early foreign aid
questions.explanation: The passage covers the destruction, slow aid, and differing explanations for the difficult recovery.

questions.passage: In many Filipino homes, a younger person greets an elder by taking the elder's hand and pressing it to the forehead. This gesture, called mano, is accompanied by the words "Mano po." The elder usually replies with a blessing. Outsiders sometimes mistake the custom for a mere formality, but for Filipinos it expresses gratitude and respect for the experience elders carry. Children first learn the custom by imitation, long before they can explain it. By the time they are adults, many perform it without thinking, much like a handshake elsewhere.

questions.passage: The town council was divided over the proposal to close the old market for renovation. Supporters, mostly shop owners with newer stalls, pointed to leaking roofs and fire hazards. questions.passage: Scientists once believed that the human brain stopped forming new connections after childhood. Research over recent decades has overturned this view. Learning a language, practicing an instrument, or even navigating a new city can strengthen existing connections and build new ones, a property called neuroplasticity. The changes are gradual and demand effort; a few days of casual study will not rewire anything. Nevertheless, the finding is encouraging, because it suggests that adults who feel too old to learn a new skill may be underestimating themselves.

options: Children learn more quickly than adults.
The adult brain can still change through sustained learning.
questions.explanation: Research shows connections can strengthen and form in adults, with effort.

questions.passage: When Kuya Mark was promoted to supervisor, his office mates expected little to change. He still ate lunch with them, still joked about traffic, and still stayed late to help when deadlines loomed. But one Monday, he quietly returned a report to a close friend, noting three errors that could embarrass the whole section. The friend was hurt at first, since the mistakes seemed small. By Friday, though, the friend admitted that the client had asked about the very figures Mark had flagged. Mark said nothing, only slid a cup of coffee across the desk.

questions.passage: In 1991, the eruption of Mount Pinatubo ejected so much ash and sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere that global temperatures fell by about half a degree Celsius over the next two years. The sulfur formed tiny droplets that reflected sunlight back into space. Some researchers have proposed copying this effect deliberately to counter climate change. Critics reply that the cooling would be temporary, that it would not reduce the carbon dioxide that is acidifying the oceans, and that changing rainfall patterns might harm farmers in some regions even as others benefit. For these reasons, most scientists treat the idea as a last resort rather than a solution.
questions.question: Which is the best summary of the passage?
options: Volcanoes should be triggered on purpose.
Pinatubo erupted in 1991 and ended climate change.
Ocean acidity is caused by sulfur droplets.
A volcanic eruption cooled the Earth, but copying the effect is considered a risky and limited option.
Farmers benefit from all rainfall changes.
questions.explanation: It describes the cooling, the proposal, and the criticisms that make it a last resort.
